idiom_name: sealed trait + final case class / case object
implementation_notes: `sealed` limits extension to the same source file, which is exactly what the compiler needs to know the complete variant set, and `case class`/`case object` supply immutable, value-equal, destructurable, copyable carriers; a `match` whose scrutinee has the sealed static type is checked for exhaustiveness (a warning by default, an error with `-Xfatal-warnings`), and each added case points at every match that needs review. Because `sealed` is not transitive and case classes are final, closure holds only if each case is a `final case class` or `case object`; `sealed abstract class` is often used as the base where Java interoperation or marginally cheaper dispatch matters, while a trait base lets cases mix in other behaviours. This form still compiles under Scala 3, so it remains the right choice for cross-built libraries and for cases that need extra traits.
pitfalls: `sealed` is not transitive: matching on the type of a *case* (not the sealed base) silently loses the exhaustiveness check, and extending a case reopens the set unless it is `final`.
Exhaustiveness is a warning by default; without `-Xfatal-warnings` a missing case ships, and a `case _ =>` arm defeats the check entirely.
The whole hierarchy must live in one file, which forces layout compromises for large vocabularies.
Case classes are only shallowly immutable: an `Array`/mutable-collection field can still change, and `copy` shares that field with the original.

variants.name: Scala 3 enum with parameterized cases
variants.implementation_notes: Scala 3's `enum` is sugar for a sealed class plus a companion object holding the cases - parameterized cases become `case class`es, nullary cases become singleton values - and it adds utilities such as `values`/`fromOrdinal`. It is the concise form when all cases are pure data and no case needs to extend anything but universal traits; the explicit sealed-trait form remains the choice when cases must mix in other traits, when the code is cross-built with Scala 2, or when the closure needs `sealed abstract class` interop. Case analysis is the same `match` with an exhaustiveness warning.
variants.code_sketch:
enum Payment:
  case Card(number: String)
  case Transfer(iban: String)

def describe(p: Payment): String = p match
  case Payment.Card(number)   => number
  case Payment.Transfer(iban) => iban
pitfalls: Enums cannot extend classes (only universal traits), so a case that needs a shared base implementation must use the sealed-trait form.
Cases live in the enum's companion object (`Payment.Card`), which changes import and pattern syntax compared with top-level case classes.

`enum` is Scala 3-only, so a codebase cross-built with Scala 2 must keep the sealed-trait form; an enum's cases are also final, so the hierarchy can never be reopened for a test double or an extended case.
